extracted.intended_audience: botanists, naturalists, and readers interested in floral morphology and insect pollination
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and generalisations for assessing how papilionaceous (pea‑family) flowers are structurally adapted for insect pollination, based on morphology of petals, stamens, styles, nectar placement, and orientation. Includes examples across genera (Pisum, Vicia, Lathyrus, Lupin, Ulex, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Position of flowers in blossom
rubrics_metrics.description: "The position of the flowers in blossom, whatever their other wants and habits, is such as to make them attractive and convenient to insects. In general the showy vexillum is upright, and the keel and wings horizontal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains adaptive orientations and lists mechanisms that effect it (raising/straightening of the stalk as in Pisum and Lathyrus; lowering of it as in Faba, Phaseolus, and Ulex; giving the pedicel a half twist as in Robinia, Wistaria, and Laburnum). Purpose: to afford good access/lighting for insect visitors seeking nectar and to position reproductive organs for contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohesion of petals correlated with nectary position, fertilising apparatus, and pollen nature
rubrics_metrics.description: "The cohesion of the petals (which in this single tribe is so various) is in each flower correlated to the position of the nectary, the structure of the fertilising apparatus, and the nature of the pollen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives genus-level examples: Ulex/Genista/Sarothamnus — minimal petal cohesion, wings not adherent to keel, open keel, dusty pollen; Pisum/Vicia/Lathyrus/Phaseolus — wings often unite with keel and help force out pollen; Trifolium — maximum cohesion producing a long tube containing much nectar; Anthyllis — calyx forms nectary while petal claws are free. Use this correlation to interpret function from petal cohesion patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of stamen cohesion depends on necessity for access to nectar
rubrics_metrics.description: "The degree to which the cohesion of the stamens is carried ... appears to depend on the necessity for access to nectar."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational rule: where stamens are monadelphous (Ulex, Sarothamnus, Genista, Cytisus, Ononis, Lupin) there is generally no nectar in the staminal tube and no space/access; where the tenth stamen is free or separated at the base (allowing insect access to staminal tube) a cavity for nectar within the staminal tube is often present. Notes Darwin's symmetry comment explaining double apertures at stamen base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filament, anther and pollen structure relate to insect‑fertilisation function
rubrics_metrics.description: "Other points in the structure of the filaments, anthers, and pollen seem also to be more or less related to and to depend upon the same function of fertilisation by insects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies patterns and examples: stiff filaments in Ulex, Genista, Sarothamnus and in Lupin/Lotus where filaments drive pollen out; limp filaments in Phaseolus where the style performs that function. Notes dilated or wedge-shaped filament tips (Lupin, Lotus) that collect and push pollen; contrasts moist (sticky) pollen accompanied by apparatus to sweep it out, versus dusty pollen that is simply exposed and brushes onto insects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of style and stigma adapted to contact with entering insects and to sweeping pollen
rubrics_metrics.description: "The structure of the style and stigma is in every case adapted so as to bring the latter in contact with an entering insect... the most peculiar function of the style in many of these flowers is that of sweeping out the moist pollen of its own flower from the keel."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details placement and form of brushes/hairs and mechanical actions: brush on inside of style in Pisum; on both sides in Lathyrus; all round but more thickly on insect side in Phaseolus; on outside in Vicia; at the extremity in Lupin. Includes style recoil mechanisms (e.g., Sarothamnus) and emergence from spiral keel (Phaseolus) as ways the stigma contacts insects and/or sweeps pollen out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nectar location varies but is arranged so an insect seeking nectar touches stigma and carries pollen
rubrics_metrics.description: "The nectar is found in various parts of the flower—within the staminal tube, in the vexillum, and in the calyx. But in all cases the correlation of the parts is such that an insect seeking the nectar must touch the stigma and carry away pollen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/location of nectar (staminal tube, vexillum, calyx) together with petal and reproductive organ architecture to predict whether nectar‑seeking visitors will contact stigma/anthers. Examples: nectar in staminal tube when tenth stamen separated; vexillum or calyx nectaries in other genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific pollen‑presentation and release mechanisms (keel opening, dilated filaments, style recoil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of mechanical devices by which pollen is presented to insects: e.g., dilated filament tops in Lupin that, upon keel pressure, push pollen out; keel acting as a hinge and opening (Sarothamnus, Ulex) causing anthers to project and dust insects; style recoil that brings stigma into contact with subsequent visitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides genus-specific mechanistic examples and observations: Lupin — five inner filaments dilated as wedges that collect and push pollen; Sarothamnus — keel opens and style coils to bring stigma to insect; Ulex — bees push keel, anthers project and dust body; Phaseolus — spiral keel and emergence of style. These mechanisms should be used as functional criteria when evaluating floral adaptation to insect-mediated pollen transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for exceptions and need for further observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes an apparent exception (Coronilla) and absence of sufficient observations: "there is one genus, Coronilla, which... forms an exception to the above generalisation; but I have not been able to procure sufficient flowers to enable me to state any positive conclusion with respect to this genus."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the generalisations as empirically grounded but open to exceptions; encourage additional observational verification across genera and localities when applying these criteria.
